preferences.label: Which programming languages do you prefer?
preferences.help: Pick any you like reading or already know a little. Agents write the code either way — this just steers what the code is written in.

preferences.label: Preferred package manager?
preferences.help: The tool that installs a project's dependencies. If unsure, 'No preference' picks the standard one for your language.

preferences.label: Default license for your projects?
preferences.help: Controls what others may do with your code. MIT is the permissive default; 'Proprietary' keeps all rights.

preferences.label: Preferred testing tool?
preferences.help: How automated checks run against the code. Agents write tests regardless; this picks the runner.

preferences.label: Continuous integration?
preferences.help: A service that runs your tests automatically on every change. GitHub Actions is free for public repos.

preferences.label: Code formatting / linting?
preferences.help: Keeps all code looking consistent so diffs stay readable. Safe to leave to the planner.

preferences.label: Web UI framework?
preferences.help: The library that builds what users see in the browser. React has the biggest ecosystem; HTMX and plain HTML keep things simplest.

preferences.label: Meta-framework or build tool?
preferences.help: The scaffolding around the UI framework: dev server, routing, bundling. Vite is the light default; Next/Nuxt/SvelteKit add server rendering.

preferences.label: How should styling be done?
preferences.help: How the app gets its look. Tailwind is popular with agents and humans alike; plain CSS is the zero-dependency option.

preferences.label: State management?
preferences.help: How the app keeps track of data on screen. Built-ins are enough for most apps — only pick a library if you know you want it.

preferences.label: Backend pairing for web apps?
preferences.help: The server side that stores data and enforces rules. 'No separate backend' means a static site or serverless-only app.

preferences.label: Database for web apps?
preferences.help: Where the app's data lives. PostgreSQL is the safe general choice; SQLite is a single file with zero setup — great for small apps.

preferences.label: Database access layer (ORM)?
preferences.help: How code talks to the database. An ORM adds convenience and type-safety; raw SQL keeps things transparent.

preferences.label: How should sign-in work?
preferences.help: How people prove who they are. Email + password in your own database is simplest to own; hosted providers offload the hard parts.

preferences.label: Where should web apps be hosted?
preferences.help: Where the app runs on the internet. Most of these have free tiers good enough for small apps.

preferences.label: Mobile app approach?
preferences.help: One codebase for both platforms (React Native, Flutter) is cheapest; native apps feel most polished; a PWA skips app stores entirely.

preferences.label: Backend for mobile apps?
preferences.help: Where the mobile app's data lives. Reusing the same backend as your web app avoids building things twice.
options: Same backend as my web app

preferences.label: Navigation library?
preferences.help: How the app moves between screens. Safe to leave to the planner — it follows your framework choice.

preferences.label: How will the app reach phones?
preferences.help: App stores reach everyone but require developer accounts and review; internal/TestFlight is fine for a small group; a PWA installs from the browser.

preferences.label: Language for backend services?
preferences.help: The language your API is written in. TypeScript and Python have the most examples; Go and Rust run leaner.

preferences.label: API framework?
preferences.help: The library that handles requests. This should match your language choice — 'No preference' lets the planner pair them sensibly.

preferences.label: API style?
preferences.help: The shape of the interface. REST with JSON is the boring default almost everything understands.

preferences.label: Database for services?
preferences.help: The service's system of record. PostgreSQL is the safe general answer; SQLite is great for single-server apps.

preferences.label: Caching layer?
preferences.help: Speeds up repeated reads. Most small apps don't need one — 'None needed' is a perfectly good answer.

preferences.label: Background jobs / queue?
preferences.help: For work that shouldn't block a request (emails, imports). Database-backed jobs avoid adding infrastructure.

preferences.label: API documentation?
preferences.help: How other people (or your own frontend) learn what the API does. OpenAPI generates interactive docs from the code.

preferences.label: Where should services run?
preferences.help: Where the API lives in production. Fly/Render/Railway are simple; AWS/GCP/Azure scale further but ask more of you.

preferences.label: Language for command-line tools?
preferences.help: Go and Rust produce single-file binaries anyone can run; Node and Python are quickest to iterate on.

preferences.label: Argument parsing library?
preferences.help: How the tool reads flags like --help and --verbose. Safe to leave to the planner — it follows your language choice.

preferences.label: How should CLI tools be distributed?
preferences.help: How other people install your tool. npm/PyPI if they have the runtime; prebuilt binaries or Homebrew if they don't.

preferences.label: Language for data work?
preferences.help: Python owns the data ecosystem; SQL-first (dbt) fits when the data already lives in a warehouse.

preferences.label: Notebooks or pipelines?
preferences.help: Notebooks are great for exploring; pipelines are repeatable scripts you can schedule. Many projects start as one and become the other.

preferences.label: Scheduling / orchestration?
preferences.help: What runs your data jobs on a schedule. Cron (or none) is plenty until you have many interdependent jobs.

preferences.label: Where should data live?
preferences.help: DuckDB and SQLite are single files with serious query power; warehouses (BigQuery/Snowflake) suit team-scale data.

preferences.label: Charts and dashboards?
preferences.help: How results get seen. Streamlit turns a Python script into a small web app; Metabase/Grafana are point-and-click dashboards.

interview.label: What are you building?
interview.help: Describe it the way you would to a friend — what it does, and why you want it to exist. Plain English beats jargon.
interview.placeholder: A small web app where my friends and I keep shared todo lists — groceries, trip planning — and everyone sees updates.

interview.label: Who will use it?
interview.help: The actual people: just you, your family, a team at work, paying customers?

interview.label: What kind of app is it?
interview.help: Pick everything that applies — lots of projects are a web app plus an API behind it. 'Not sure' is a fine answer.

interview.label: What are the 3–5 must-have features?
interview.help: The things version 1 cannot ship without. Everything else can wait for version 2.
interview.placeholder: 1. Shared lists  2. Invite a friend by link  3. Check items off  4. Works on phones

interview.label: What does it need to connect to?
interview.help: Other services, APIs, data sources, or files it must read or write — or nothing at all.
interview.placeholder: Nothing external — maybe email for invites later

interview.label: Do people need to sign in?
interview.help: Sign-in adds real work, so only ask for what you need. 'Not sure' lets the plan recommend the simplest thing that fits.

interview.label: How many people will use it?
interview.help: Small is a feature — it unlocks simpler, cheaper choices for hosting and databases.
options: A small group (friends, family, my team)

interview.label: Any constraints?
interview.help: Budget limits, hosting requirements, privacy rules, deadlines, devices it must run on — anything the plan must respect.
interview.placeholder: Free or nearly-free hosting; my friends' data shouldn't be sold to anyone

interview.label: It's done when…
interview.help: Describe the concrete moment you'd call version 1 finished. The more checkable, the better the plan.
interview.placeholder: Two of us check off groceries on the same list from our own phones, and it just works

interview.label: What should the project folder be called?
interview.help: PlanForge creates this folder next to your other projects and sets up git inside it. Leave blank to name it after the plan.

interview.label: Create a GitHub repository for it?
interview.help: The build pool opens and merges pull requests, so it needs a GitHub repo. Private is a safe default; you can skip this and add one later.

interview.label: Anything else the plan should know?
interview.help: Names you like, look and feel, things you tried before that didn't work, strong opinions — anything at all.
